days.title: Connection Architecture and Sync Patterns

concepts.heading: Direct connections versus agents
concepts.body: Data Connection brings external data into Foundry through a source (the connection and its credentials) and syncs that copy data into datasets. When Foundry can reach the source over the network, a direct connection is the simplest choice because it needs no extra host to run. When the source sits inside a closed corporate network that cannot be opened to inbound traffic, an agent is installed on a host inside that network; it reaches the local systems and connects outbound to the platform to run the syncs. For many separate closed networks, plan one agent per network with standard configuration and central health monitoring. The exam rewards the simplest architecture that works: agents are the answer to unreachable sources, not a default.

concepts.heading: Match the connector to how the source delivers data
concepts.body: Pick the ingestion route by the source's interface rather than by habit. Files on a server such as SFTP fit a file-based sync that lands new files in a raw dataset; databases fit a JDBC-style table sync; REST APIs fit an API source whose sync handles authentication, pagination and incremental parameters within the provider's rate limit; continuous event streams such as a Kafka topic fit a streaming sync. Systems that push events to the platform need push-based streaming ingestion with a declared payload schema. Unusual file formats (archives, fixed-width layouts) are best landed unchanged by a file sync and then parsed in a versioned transform with expectations. When two interfaces could work, compare completeness, rate limits, schema stability and operating cost.

concepts.heading: Snapshot, append, update and CDC syncs
concepts.body: A snapshot sync copies the whole source each run; it is always correct and is the right answer for small or slowly changing tables, or whenever there is no reliable change signal. An append sync fetches only rows added since the last run, keyed on an increasing column such as a transaction id, and suits insert-only sources. An update sync uses a change signal like an `updated_at` timestamp to fetch inserts and updates, but it is only as good as that signal: if the source edits rows without advancing it, those rows are silently missed. Change data capture (CDC) reads the source's change log and replicates inserts, updates and deletes without needing a timestamp column, which suits large tables that change often and need low latency. With CDC the raw dataset holds change events, so a downstream keyed transform must apply all of them, including deletes, to produce current state.

concepts.heading: Watermarks, late rows and deletions
concepts.body: Incremental syncs depend on a monotonic watermark, so prefer UTC timestamps, commit timestamps or sequence numbers over local time, which can jump with daylight-saving changes. Rows that arrive late can be caught with a lookback window that re-reads a little before the last watermark, combined with deduplication on the primary key. If a source change breaks monotonicity, switch to a better signal or to CDC and reconcile the rows that were missed. Append-only and update syncs never see deletions by themselves; capture them with CDC, a periodic key-only snapshot compared against the data, or a soft-delete flag in the source. A periodic reconciliation run is a cheap safety net for any incremental pattern.

examPoints: When a scenario describes a source Foundry cannot reach and a network that will not be opened, prefer an agent inside that network that connects outbound; when the source is reachable, prefer a direct connection and avoid the extra host.

When a scenario describes a table with no trustworthy change column, prefer a snapshot sync (or CDC if deletes and low latency matter) over an update sync, because an incremental pattern needs something reliable to key on.

quiz.q: An insert-only ledger table has a strictly increasing entry number and is several hundred million rows long. Which sync pattern fits best?
choices: An append sync that fetches only entries numbered above the last one ingested
A full snapshot sync every hour so that the dataset always mirrors the table
A CDC sync, because every large table needs its change log replicated
An update sync keyed on the local wall-clock time when each row was read
quiz.explain: Insert-only data with an increasing key is the textbook case for an append sync; snapshots waste work at this size, and CDC adds change-log replication that an insert-only source does not need.

quiz.q: A nightly update sync keyed on a modification timestamp keeps missing some corrected rows, although each run succeeds. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The agent host is too small to hold the full table in memory
The source changes those rows without advancing the modification timestamp
The downstream transform reads the dataset before the sync commits
The dataset needs a larger number of output files to store corrections
quiz.explain: An update sync selects rows only through its change signal; if the source edits rows without moving that signal, the rows are never selected, so fix the signal or move to CDC and reconcile.

days.recap: Choose the connection (direct or agent) by reachability, the connector by the source's interface, and the sync pattern (snapshot, append, update, CDC) by the change signal, change types and latency the requirement needs.

days.title: Virtual Tables, Governed Exports and Diagnosing Ingestion

concepts.heading: Virtual tables: use data without copying it
concepts.body: A virtual table registers an external table (for example a cloud warehouse table) in Foundry and queries it in place, so the data stays at the source. It is the right answer when policy says the data must not be copied, or when a team wants to explore before committing to ingestion. Cost and speed depend on the queries sent to the source, so shape them with filters, column selection and pushdown, and materialize a curated subset in Foundry for frequent analyses if policy allows. The source sees one shared connection credential, so there is no identity federation: when objects backed by a virtual table look different for different users, the difference comes from Foundry-side controls such as object security policies. If every user suddenly gets authentication errors, the shared credential has probably expired or been rotated and must be updated in the source configuration.

concepts.heading: Governed exports and egress
concepts.body: Data leaves the platform through configured exports to approved destinations under egress policies, never through ad hoc code, personal downloads or email. A good pattern is to build a partner-specific or regulatory extract as its own dataset that contains exactly the permitted rows and columns, enforce its schema with an expectation, and deliver it through a logged export. Lineage from the extract back to its sources, plus the export's execution history and approval records, gives auditors a complete trail. Credentials for sources never belong in transform code; they live in the Data Connection source configuration, and transforms read the synced datasets.

concepts.heading: Diagnosing stale or failing ingestion
concepts.body: Stale outputs while downstream builds succeed point upstream: a successful build on unchanged input simply reproduces yesterday's result. Start with the sync's execution history and error, then the agent's health and the source credentials, before touching any transform. Some symptoms map to specific causes: exactly one page of records from an API means pagination is not configured; successful runs with zero new rows mean the incremental condition or filter no longer matches anything; a sync that waits on its source suggests a dropped index, source load or a changed query plan. Intermittent agent failures are diagnosed by correlating failure times with agent health, host resources, source load and network stability. Files that are still being written should not be picked up, so require a completion signal such as a marker file, rename after write or minimum file age.

concepts.heading: Schema drift and monitoring built in from day one
concepts.body: When a source adds a column, classify the change as additive, update the sync's expected schema deliberately, validate downstream transforms on a branch and rerun; never delete and recreate datasets to make an error go away. For unreliable sources, design layers: tolerant landing of raw data, parsing that absorbs additive drift but fails on breaking drift, key-based deduplication, realistic checks and a quarantine path. Every new sync should come with Data Health checks for status, freshness and size, agent health monitoring and alerts routed to the owning team. Onboarding sources through a standard template (owner, credentials, landing dataset, documented keys, expectations, health checks, alerts and a runbook) turns ingestion into a manageable fleet.

examPoints: When a scenario says data must stay at the source or a team only wants to explore it, prefer a virtual table over any form of copy, and look at Foundry-side policies when results differ by user.
When a scenario reports stale outputs but green downstream builds, prefer checking the sync's execution history, agent health and credentials first, rather than rebuilding downstream or tuning Spark.

quiz.q: A partner needs a weekly file containing six approved columns from a curated dataset. Which approach fits the platform's governance model?
choices: Let the partner read the full curated dataset and filter the columns themselves
Write a transform that emails the file to the partner from inside the code
Build an extract dataset with only the approved columns and deliver it through a governed export under the egress policy
Download the dataset once a week and upload it to the partner's server by hand
quiz.explain: External delivery goes through a scoped extract and a logged, policy-governed export; giving wider access or moving data by hand or by code bypasses those controls.

quiz.q: Every user querying a virtual table suddenly receives authentication errors, although nobody changed Foundry permissions. What should be checked first?
choices: Each user's project role on the project that holds the virtual table
Whether the dataset needs to be converted into a full snapshot copy
The Spark details of the last build that read the virtual table
The shared connection credential in the source configuration, which may have expired or been rotated
quiz.explain: The source sees one connection credential for everyone, so an all-users authentication failure points to that credential, which is rotated in the governed source configuration.

days.recap: Keep data at the source with virtual tables, move it out only through governed exports, and diagnose ingestion by following the evidence upstream to the sync, agent and credentials before changing anything downstream.

days.title: Authoring Tools and Core Transformations

concepts.heading: Pipeline Builder, Code Repositories or Code Workspaces
concepts.body: The exam guide asks you to choose the authoring tool by complexity, team skills, custom libraries and processing needs. Pipeline Builder is visual authoring for standard joins, unions, filters, expressions and aggregations, with branching, scheduling and lineage, so it suits non-programmers and standard logic. Code Repositories hold code transforms (for example Python or SQL) with unit tests, declared dependencies on custom libraries and full control, so they suit complex or library-dependent logic and engineering teams. Code Workspaces are interactive notebooks for exploration and model development, not the primary home of production pipelines. Mixing tools is fine: keep standard steps visual and move complex, reusable logic into tested code.

concepts.heading: From exploration to a production pipeline
concepts.body: Logic that started in an exploratory analysis (for example in Contour) should be re-implemented as a governed pipeline with expectations, lineage and a schedule, using the analysis as the specification. Large pipelines are easier to operate when split into stages with intermediate datasets and contracts: parsing to a typed dataset, business rules to curated data, then shaping for the Ontology. Logic needed by several teams should be implemented once, as a shared dataset or code library, rather than copied into each project. When migrating an implementation from one tool to another, rebuild it on a branch and compare outputs on the same inputs before switching consumers.

concepts.heading: Joins, unions and aggregations at the right grain
concepts.body: Use a union when the inputs have the same structure and you want more rows, after aligning column names, order and types; use a join when related rows add columns. When a join unexpectedly multiplies rows, check whether the key is unique on the side that should be unique and fix the data or the join contract, rather than hiding the problem with a deduplication step. Per-entity metrics are group-by aggregations at the entity's grain joined back to the entity dataset, and a left join from the full population with an explicit default (such as zero) keeps entities without activity. Agree how nulls are treated in aggregates and make missing data visible, for example by reporting null counts.

concepts.heading: Windows, keys and specialized enrichment
concepts.body: Window functions handle calculations that depend on row order within a group: lag for the previous reading per sensor, ranking to keep the latest address per customer, or a range frame for a rolling seven-day sum. Fuzzy matches need normalized join keys (case, punctuation, abbreviations), a measured match rate and an explicit path for unmatched rows. Deduplicate on the business identity, not on shared attributes, and send ambiguous matches to review. Specialized steps exist for specialized data: point-in-polygon joins for "inside this area" rules, media-aware transforms for images, and structured LLM enrichment with enumerated output for text-to-category tasks. Semi-structured JSON is handled by promoting common attributes to typed columns while keeping the raw column for the long tail.

examPoints: When a scenario features analysts without coding skills building standard joins and filters, prefer Pipeline Builder; when it needs custom libraries, unit tests or complex logic, prefer Code Repositories.
When a scenario shows a join producing more rows than expected, prefer checking key uniqueness and cardinality over adding a deduplication step that masks the defect.

quiz.q: Three regional files have the same columns except that one names a column differently. The team wants one dataset with all rows. What is the right operation?
choices: Rename the odd column, align column order and types, then union the three inputs with a region column
Join the three files on their row numbers so that columns line up side by side
Aggregate each file by region first and then join the three aggregates together
Load each file into a separate object type and combine them in the application
quiz.explain: Same structure and more rows calls for a union after aligning schemas; a join is for adding columns from related rows.

quiz.q: A team must compute, for each customer and day, the total spend over the preceding seven days. Which technique fits?
choices: A self-join of every order to every other order of the same customer
A window function partitioned by customer, ordered by date, with a seven-day range frame
A union of seven copies of the dataset, each shifted by one day
A group-by on customer alone, followed by dividing the total by seven
quiz.explain: Rolling aggregates over ordered rows within a group are what window functions with range frames are for; the other approaches are wrong or scale poorly.

days.recap: Choose the authoring tool by complexity and skills, stage large pipelines with contracts, and pick joins, unions, aggregations and windows by the grain and shape of the result you need.

days.title: Compute Engines, Testing and Debugging Transforms

concepts.heading: Lightweight or distributed compute
concepts.body: The exam guide asks you to choose a compute engine by scale, memory, API needs, startup cost and feature compatibility. Spark distributes work across executors, which pays off for data beyond one node's memory, but every run pays a distributed startup cost that can dominate small jobs. A lightweight single-node engine (typically with libraries such as pandas or Polars) suits inputs of a few megabytes and libraries that need single-node APIs. Before switching, confirm the logic does not depend on engine-specific features and compare outputs on a branch. Watch growth: when projected volume will exceed a single node, migrate to a distributed engine before the job fails.

concepts.heading: Keeping Spark work distributed and balanced
concepts.body: Collecting a large dataset to the driver to build a lookup dictionary breaks scale; replace it with a distributed join, or a broadcast join when the lookup side is small. Broadcasting a small dimension avoids shuffling a large fact table, while large-to-large joins benefit from pruning both sides early and co-partitioning on the key. One straggler task that runs far longer than the rest usually means skew on a join or group key, fixed by salting or repartitioning the hot key rather than buying a bigger cluster. Output file counts are controlled by repartitioning to a sensible partition count before writing. Spark details confirm each of these diagnoses.

concepts.heading: A successful build is not a correct result
concepts.body: When numbers disagree with the business definition, reproduce the job on a branch with the same inputs and compare intermediate counts and sums step by step until the gap appears. Date logic is a frequent culprit: time zones and inclusive or exclusive period ends shift rows between periods. Non-deterministic logic, such as taking the "first" row without an explicit order, can change between runs because it depends on partitioning; give every ordered selection a sort key with a tie-breaker. A new null bucket in a report usually means a broken mapping upstream, so trace it with lineage, fix it and add a non-null expectation.

concepts.heading: Tests, expectations and reviewed changes
concepts.body: Critical transforms are protected by several layers together: unit tests on transformation functions covering typical, edge and bad inputs; expectations on outputs that enforce schema, keys and reconciliation to a control figure; a branch build compared with production by counts, keys and values; and required review before merge. Refactors are validated the same way, by building on a branch and comparing the full output with the current version. Business parameters that change, such as thresholds or alias lists, belong in a governed reference dataset read at build time rather than hard-coded in the transform. Exclusion logic should be explicit, with named steps or a reason column, so it is testable. Versioned code, builds tied to commits and lineage give automatic provenance.

examPoints: When a scenario shows a small input where distributed startup dominates runtime, prefer a lightweight engine; when data exceeds one node's memory or will soon, prefer Spark.
When a scenario asks how to validate a refactor or a critical transform change, prefer a branch build compared with production plus tests and expectations over merging because the build succeeded.

quiz.q: In a Spark build, one task of a join stage runs for forty minutes while the other tasks finish in under a minute. What is the most likely cause and fix?
choices: The cluster is undersized, so the fix is to double the executor count
The input has too few files, so the fix is to append more files
A hot key is skewing the join, so the fix is to salt or repartition that key and confirm in Spark details
The output has too many columns, so the fix is to drop unused properties
quiz.explain: One straggler task is the classic skew signature; fixing the key distribution addresses it, while adding resources leaves the one overloaded task in place.

quiz.q: A transform picks each customer's "first" order without an explicit ordering, and results differ between identical runs. What should the engineer do?
choices: Run the build twice and keep whichever output matches last month
Switch to a lightweight engine so that partitioning no longer matters
Add a deduplication step on all columns after the selection
Give the selection an explicit sort key with a tie-breaker so the result is deterministic
quiz.explain: Without explicit ordering the chosen row depends on how data is partitioned; a defined sort key with a tie-breaker makes the transform deterministic.

days.recap: Pick the engine by scale and startup cost, keep Spark work distributed and balanced, and prove correctness with tests, expectations and branch comparisons rather than trusting a green build.

days.title: Choosing a Processing Mode and Transaction Semantics

concepts.heading: Batch, incremental, streaming or lightweight
concepts.body: The core decision is batch, incremental, streaming or lightweight, chosen by freshness, volume, growth, source behaviour, complexity and cost. Start by eliciting the real requirement: what decision depends on the data and how quickly it must reflect new events. Batch recomputation from full history suits periodic authoritative outputs such as a month-end report run after inputs are final. Incremental processing suits large inputs that grow by appends with a daily or sub-daily freshness need. Streaming is reserved for decisions that must happen within seconds of an event, such as card fraud checks, and it brings state, backlogs and replay to manage.

concepts.heading: Combining modes
concepts.body: One source can feed outputs with different freshness needs, so mixing modes is often correct: a stream for the latest vehicle positions on a map and a daily batch over the persisted events for distances. Incremental runs can be scheduled on a business cadence, for example every 15 minutes in campaign weeks and daily otherwise. When only some keys changed, recompute just those keys and merge them into the output. Many incremental designs add a periodic full recompute or a bounded recompute window to reconcile late corrections. The exam rewards the cheapest mode that meets the stated requirement, documented and monitored.

concepts.heading: SNAPSHOT, APPEND, UPDATE and DELETE
concepts.body: A Foundry dataset is a sequence of transactions, each changing the set of files in its current view. A SNAPSHOT transaction replaces the view with its own files; APPEND adds files and cannot modify existing ones; UPDATE adds or replaces files while keeping the rest; DELETE removes files. Committing an APPEND that would overwrite an existing file fails, so a writer that reuses the same output file name each run must write unique files or use UPDATE. A SNAPSHOT that contains only today's new rows hides everything else, so a writer must either append or snapshot the full intended contents. Writing a full recomputed output as one SNAPSHOT replaces the view atomically, so consumers never see partial state.

concepts.heading: Designing writes around the semantics
concepts.body: Incremental processing relies on APPEND inputs, and a pipeline is only as incremental as its weakest link, so each transform in the chain should write APPEND transactions where possible. Append-only ingestion never removes rows; deletions need CDC with deletes, periodic snapshots or a soft-delete flag. An APPEND file sync ingests files not yet ingested, keyed by file path, so the same content re-delivered under a new path is appended twice; guard against it with key-based deduplication and a uniqueness expectation. When both an audit trail and current state are required, keep an append-only history dataset and derive a current-state dataset from it. Small recurring corrections can be appended as keyed correction records and merged downstream.

examPoints: When a scenario gives a daily freshness need on a large append-only input, prefer incremental processing over streaming or a full nightly recompute.
When a scenario shows rows vanishing from a dataset after a run that wrote only new rows, suspect a partial SNAPSHOT and prefer APPEND for additions or a SNAPSHOT of the full contents.

quiz.q: A dataset received a SNAPSHOT with files one and two on Monday, an APPEND with file three on Tuesday, and a DELETE of file two on Wednesday. Which files are in the current view?
choices: Files one and three
Files one, two and three
Only file three
Only file one
quiz.explain: Apply transactions in order: the snapshot sets files one and two, the append adds file three, and the delete removes file two.

quiz.q: A business owner asks for "real-time" sales figures, but on questioning they review them once each morning. Which mode should the engineer choose?
choices: A streaming pipeline, since the owner used the word real-time
An incremental or batch run that completes before the morning review
A lightweight engine with no schedule, built manually when needed
Separate streaming and batch pipelines producing two competing datasets
quiz.explain: The real requirement is morning freshness, so the cheapest mode that meets it is a scheduled batch or incremental run; streaming would add cost and operational burden for nothing.

days.recap: Choose the simplest processing mode that meets the real freshness need, and design every write around SNAPSHOT, APPEND, UPDATE and DELETE semantics so incremental consumers stay incremental.

days.title: Incremental Fallback, Streaming State and Replay

concepts.heading: How incremental transforms work and when they fall back
concepts.body: An incremental transform processes the input transactions added since its last successful run, which is well defined when inputs grow by APPEND. SNAPSHOT, UPDATE and DELETE transactions on an input change or remove earlier data, so they can make the transform fall back to a full recompute for that run. When an incremental build suddenly runs as a snapshot, inspect the input's transaction history for one of those transactions. Upstream transaction types are therefore part of the contract with incremental consumers: switching a sync to snapshot mode forces every consumer to recompute fully, so coordinate such changes. Retention deletions also cause fallback, so materialize any aggregates that must outlive the raw data before deleting it.

concepts.heading: Fallback-aware state, idempotency and validation
concepts.body: Running state, such as a cumulative total, must be rebuilt rather than combined with a fallback recompute, or the result double counts. Incremental transforms should be idempotent: processing an increment once or several times must give the same output, which keyed merges or deduplication achieve. Validate an incremental design on a branch against the batch result over several runs, including one after an upstream UPDATE. Backfill history in validated chunks without interrupting live incremental runs. Do not add incremental complexity before it pays off: a batch job that meets its window can stay batch, with a runtime trigger to revisit.

concepts.heading: Corrections, late data and small files
concepts.body: When sources send corrections, publish a documented current-state view built by merging corrections by key, optionally alongside an append history. Late data is handled with a bounded recompute window, for example re-processing the last seven days by event date, plus periodic reconciliation. Reference data changes are treated as deliberate recomputes of the affected range while routine runs stay incremental. Frequent incremental writes produce many small files that slow reads, so add periodic compaction rather than giving up frequent ingestion. File count is a performance variable worth monitoring.

concepts.heading: Streaming state, lag and replay
concepts.body: Streaming pipelines keep state, so bound it with windows, time-to-live or watermark-based cleanup; otherwise state for finished periods grows forever. A stream that runs but produces nothing is diagnosed through its lag and backlog metrics and error logs: it may be behind, stuck on a bad record or blocked on state. Lag that grows under afternoon load and recovers at night means throughput is below the input rate, so scale or reduce per-event cost and alert on lag. After an outage, replay retained messages from the last checkpoint with idempotent processing, and prepare for the burst with capacity, event-time handling and lag monitoring. Exactly-once effects come from unique event ids, bounded deduplication and idempotent updates.

concepts.heading: Event time and schema evolution in streams
concepts.body: Windows should use event time with allowed lateness set from the observed delay, and anything later should go to a late-data reconciliation path rather than being silently dropped. Long-horizon aggregates are better computed in batch over the persisted stream than held in streaming state. Slowly changing reference data, such as customer tiers, is joined in-stream through a lookup that refreshes when the reference dataset updates. Stream schemas evolve additively: make new fields optional so old and new records coexist, with tolerant consumers. Any schema change is classified first and rolled out with branch validation and consumer communication.

examPoints: When a scenario shows an incremental build that suddenly reprocessed full history, prefer inspecting the input's transaction history for a SNAPSHOT, UPDATE or DELETE over rewriting the transform.
When a scenario describes a recovered streaming outage, prefer replay from the last good checkpoint with idempotent processing over skipping the gap or restarting from scratch without deduplication.

quiz.q: After an upstream team re-ran their sync in snapshot mode, a running total produced by an incremental transform became roughly double the true value. What went wrong?
choices: The output was written as APPEND, which always doubles totals
The schedule ran twice, so the transform needs a longer interval
The fallback recompute was combined with the old running-total state instead of rebuilding it
The input files were too small and must be compacted before each run
quiz.explain: A snapshot input forces a full recompute; if the transform adds that recompute to its existing state it double counts, so state must be fallback-aware and reconciled.

quiz.q: A streaming job's memory keeps rising day after day because it holds state for every past day it has ever seen. What is the right fix?
choices: Restart the job every night so that memory is cleared
Move the job to a lightweight single-node engine
Increase executor memory each time the job approaches its limit
Add a time-to-live or watermark-based cleanup so completed windows are emitted and released
quiz.explain: Streaming state must be bounded; watermarks or TTLs emit finished windows and drop their state, whereas restarts and bigger memory only postpone the problem.

days.recap: Keep incremental transforms incremental with APPEND inputs, idempotent and fallback-aware state, and run streams with bounded state, lag monitoring and checkpoint replay.

days.title: Schedules, Triggers and Diagnostic Evidence

concepts.heading: Schedule by data arrival, not by guesswork
concepts.body: Pipelines are best scheduled as dependency graphs: trigger on the update of root inputs and build datasets in dependency order, instead of independent timers per dataset that guess when upstream work finishes. An event-based schedule can wait until all required inputs have updated since the last run, or fire when any of them updates with a minimum interval to avoid rapid repeated builds. Conditions can be combined in one schedule, such as building on input update but not before a given hour. Skip work when inputs are unchanged. Pair arrival-based triggers with a freshness alert before the business deadline, so a late source is noticed in time.

concepts.heading: Fitting schedules to consumers and capacity
concepts.body: Build frequency should follow how consumers actually use the data: hourly during business hours and once overnight may serve users as well as round-the-clock builds at far lower cost. Irregular sources such as finance feeds that only arrive on business days need input-update triggers and calendar-aware freshness checks. Heavy independent jobs that contend for compute should be staggered or sequenced, and when workloads compete for a deadline, run the deadline-bound pipeline first or on reserved capacity. Intermittent "not found" input errors usually mean a read overlapped an in-progress upstream write, which triggering on the upstream commit solves.

concepts.heading: Lineage and input comparison
concepts.body: Data Lineage shows how datasets connect, so it is the tool for walking upstream from a wrong value to the first stage that differs between two builds. A row-count drop with unchanged code is an input problem: compare the input transactions since the last good build and walk lineage to the first dataset that shrank. A "missing column" failure with unchanged code usually means an upstream rename or drop, found by comparing the input's latest schema with the previous transaction. The exam guide's playbook starts here: state the symptom, then find the first bad stage before changing anything.

concepts.heading: Spark details, Job Comparison and the Linter
concepts.body: Spark details expose stage durations, shuffle sizes, task skew, memory and input files for a build. Job Comparison puts a slow build next to a normal one, which locates what changed: more input files after a weekend of small appends, an exploding shuffle from a new duplicate join key, or a single-task output stage from writing through one partition. Heavy garbage collection near memory limits points to memory-hungry data or code, which should be reduced before adding resources. The Linter analyses pipelines and flags inefficient or risky patterns so they can be fixed before release. Together, the Linter prevents, Spark details and Job Comparison diagnose, and Data Health monitors.

examPoints: When a scenario has a pipeline that runs on a fixed timer and sometimes starts before its input lands, prefer an event-based trigger on the input update plus a freshness alert before the deadline.

When a scenario reports a build that suddenly became slow without a code change, prefer comparing it with a recent fast build through Job Comparison and Spark details over immediately adding resources.

quiz.q: A report must be rebuilt only after all three of its input datasets have refreshed each day, and they arrive at unpredictable times. Which schedule fits?
choices: An event-based schedule that waits until all three inputs have updated since the last run, then builds once
Three separate timers, one after the expected arrival of each input
A build every five minutes around the clock to catch the last arrival
A manual build triggered by whoever notices the last input arrive
quiz.explain: Waiting for every input with an event-based trigger builds exactly once, at the right moment, without guessing arrival times or wasting compute.

quiz.q: A value in a final dataset changed between two builds while the code did not change. How should the engineer locate the cause?
choices: Rebuild the final dataset several times and keep the most common value
Walk upstream with Data Lineage, comparing the value in each intermediate dataset across the two builds to find the first stage that differs
Increase the Spark memory of the final transform and rebuild
Ask consumers whether they changed any filters in their dashboards
quiz.explain: Lineage lets the engineer bisect the change through intermediate datasets to the first bad stage, which is where the repair belongs.

days.recap: Trigger builds on data arrival in dependency order, align frequency with consumers, and diagnose with lineage, input comparison, Spark details, Job Comparison and the Linter before changing anything.

days.title: Classifying Failures, Branches, Releases and Cost

concepts.heading: The troubleshooting playbook
concepts.body: The exam guide's playbook runs: state the symptom precisely, find the first bad stage, classify the failure (data, code, permissions, resources or upstream), assess the blast radius, apply the smallest safe repair, verify, communicate and add a control that prevents recurrence. Many downstream failures that share one failed input are an upstream cascade: fix the upstream dataset first, then rebuild downstream in order. Diagnose from build logs, the failing stage's error, input changes since the last good build and lineage before forming theories. Incidents should end with new expectations, health checks, alerts and runbook entries, not only a rerun.

concepts.heading: Telling failure classes apart
concepts.body: A single task failing on one file is a data problem: inspect the file, fix or quarantine it at the source and add validation so a bad file fails clearly. Intermittent memory failures that coincide with a data pattern are usually skew; fix the distribution rather than permanently buying memory. Executor disk exhaustion means shuffle spill, reduced by pre-aggregating, repartitioning or fixing skew before tuning resources. Row-wise Python UDFs on large data are slow; native dataframe functions or vectorized UDFs keep work inside the engine. Truly transient failures are absorbed with bounded automatic retries with backoff, alerting only when retries are exhausted.

concepts.heading: Permission failures in builds
concepts.body: A build runs under an executing identity, which is not necessarily the author, so an access failure is fixed by granting that identity the specific access it lacks. When reads that used to work start failing, look for a marking newly applied upstream or a change in the identity's group membership, and use Check Access to pinpoint the unmet requirement. After a pipeline or dataset moves between projects, verify that its schedule and build identity survived and still have access to inputs and outputs. Build identities get only the access their transforms need, never administrator rights for convenience.

concepts.heading: Branches, reviews and releases
concepts.body: Production pipelines change through branches: develop on a branch whose builds read production inputs but write isolated outputs, validate, review, then merge, so consumers are unaffected until the merge. Parallel work uses separate branches; an urgent fix is merged first and long-running branches stay synchronized with main. Protect main by requiring reviewed pull requests, for example when a contractor must not release unilaterally. Intentional breaking changes are coordinated releases: notify consumers found through lineage, offer a transition period with both versions, merge at an agreed time, monitor and keep a rollback path. After a bad build, dataset transaction history lets you restore a known-good version and rebuild downstream.

concepts.heading: Controlling cost
concepts.body: Cost reviews look first at unnecessary work: builds more frequent than consumption, full recomputes that could be incremental, and orphaned pipelines nobody reads. Over-partitioning creates thousands of tiny tasks for a small input; matching partition counts to data size fixes it. Right-sizing compute comes after removing unnecessary work, and fixes are prioritized by impact. A pipeline handover includes documented contracts, schedules and triggers, checks with their rationale, rerouted alerts, runbooks, a consumer list and an access review.

examPoints: When a scenario shows a build failing on access although the author can read the input, prefer granting the executing identity the specific missing access (confirmed with Check Access) over granting broad roles.

When a scenario involves changing a production pipeline or rolling back a bad output, prefer a branch with validation and review, and restoring a known-good transaction, over editing production directly.

quiz.q: Twelve downstream datasets failed overnight, and lineage shows they all depend on one curated dataset whose build failed first. What should the engineer do?
choices: Rebuild all twelve downstream datasets immediately with more memory
Disable the expectations on the downstream datasets so they build
Fix the failed curated dataset first, then rebuild the downstream datasets in dependency order
Copy yesterday's outputs into the twelve datasets by hand
quiz.explain: A shared failed input means an upstream cascade; repairing the first bad stage and rebuilding in order resolves all twelve without masking anything.

quiz.q: A small daily transform over a few megabytes launches thousands of tiny Spark tasks and costs far more than expected. What is the likely issue?
choices: The transform needs more executors to finish the tasks in parallel
The input should be streamed instead of processed in batch
The output dataset must be split into several projects
The data is over-partitioned for its size, so the partition count should be reduced
quiz.explain: Thousands of tiny tasks for a small input waste scheduling overhead; matching partitions to data size removes the waste, while more executors would add cost.

days.recap: Follow the playbook from symptom to prevention, classify failures before repairing them, change production only through validated and reviewed branches, and cut cost by removing unnecessary work first.

days.title: Expectations versus Health Checks

concepts.heading: Two layers of quality
concepts.body: The exam guide separates proactive expectations from reactive health checks. Expectations are assertions evaluated during a build (row counts, nulls, uniqueness, allowed values, schema), and a failing expectation can fail the build so the bad transaction is never committed. Health checks in Data Health watch datasets over time (freshness, schema changes, size, build status, content) and raise alerts, but they act on data that already exists. Both apply to pipelines from either authoring tool. Critical datasets usually need both: expectations to gate builds and health checks to catch drift and staleness.

concepts.heading: Block or alert: decide by consequence
concepts.body: The guide's self-check asks whether a requirement needs a blocking expectation, a health alert, or both. Block when a violation would harm consumers and has no legitimate exception, for example duplicate primary keys, an end date before a start date or a currency outside the allowed set. Alert when the condition might be legitimate, such as a 30% shift in average order value, so the team investigates without stopping the pipeline. A null that breaks a critical consumer is worth blocking; one that does not can be monitored and handled downstream. Matching blocking to consequence avoids both published bad data and needless outages.

concepts.heading: Writing expectations that encode the contract
concepts.body: Each contract rule should be its own expectation, which makes failures easy to read: key unique, key not null, amount rule conditional on order type, date not in the future. Rules that span rows, such as "a refund must not exceed its original sale", are enforced by computing a violation flag in the transform and asserting that it is never true. Allowed-value sets that evolve belong in governed reference data the business updates through review, with the expectation reading that reference. When a rule fails on legitimate data, correct the rule precisely (for example allow negative quantities only for return rows) and add a test case, rather than deleting the check.

concepts.heading: Expectations with incremental transforms
concepts.body: Expectations work with incremental transforms, but each check needs a strategy. Slice-level checks such as non-null run cheaply on the new rows of each run. Global checks such as uniqueness across all history need an incremental-aware approach: check the new slice, anti-join it against existing keys, run a full check less often, or rely on an upstream guarantee. Keep critical guarantees and make them cheaper rather than dropping them for speed. When many rules fail after a change, review each against the contract instead of removing them all.

examPoints: When a scenario describes a rule that is never legitimately violated and consumers act on the data, prefer a build-blocking expectation over a health check or a silent filter.
When a scenario describes a shift that could be a genuine business change, prefer a health check with an alert to the owner over blocking the pipeline.

quiz.q: A curated orders dataset must never publish rows whose shipping date precedes the order date, because a billing system acts on them. What control fits?
choices: A build-blocking expectation asserting the date order on every row
A weekly health check that emails a summary of violating rows
A filter in the dashboard that hides the violating rows from analysts
A note in the dataset description asking consumers to check dates
quiz.explain: An invariant with no legitimate exception that drives downstream action should stop the build before the transaction is committed.

quiz.q: What is the key behavioural difference between an expectation and a Data Health check?
choices: Expectations run only in Pipeline Builder, health checks only in Code Repositories
Expectations are evaluated during the build and can block the transaction; health checks monitor datasets over time and alert
Health checks can block builds, while expectations can only send notifications
They are identical controls with different names in different tools
quiz.explain: Expectations gate the build so bad data is never published, while health checks watch existing datasets and raise alerts; they complement each other in both authoring tools.

days.recap: Use build-blocking expectations for rules that are never legitimately broken, health checks with alerts for signals that might be legitimate, and both for critical datasets.

days.title: Blocking Invalid Data, Monitoring and Investigation

concepts.heading: When an expectation catches bad data
concepts.body: A blocking expectation that fails keeps the last good version published, which is the intended outcome: known-bad data would mislead consumers. The engineer escalates to the source owner and publishes after the fix rather than overriding the check. Referential rules stay strict on published data, while feed timing is handled with sequencing (customers before orders) and a pending dataset for rows whose references have not arrived. Non-conforming input files can be validated per file and routed to quarantine with an alert, so conforming files continue. Invalid rows can likewise go to a rejects dataset with reasons, with a cap on the reject rate.

concepts.heading: Content checks catch what build status cannot
concepts.body: A green build can carry an empty, duplicated or stale dataset, so monitoring must look at content, not just status. Row-count and size checks with expected ranges catch drops and spikes, ideally following known cycles such as day-of-week patterns. A sudden size spike usually means duplication from a multiplying join, a duplicate upstream load or a re-appended increment. A distinct-count drop with stable volume suggests identifiers collapsed to a placeholder. Distribution checks, ratios between related columns and reconciliation against an independent control total catch unit errors and semantic corruption.

concepts.heading: Freshness measured on content
concepts.body: Freshness measured only on the latest transaction time can be fooled by a build that reprocessed old data. A content-freshness check on the maximum event date, plus a freshness check on the upstream source, reveals reprocessed but stale outputs. Thresholds should follow the source's real delivery calendar, such as a longer window over weekends, so alerts fire only on genuine lateness. Schema checks should alert on removed or retyped columns while planned additive changes are absorbed through the release process.

concepts.heading: Alerts people act on
concepts.body: Noisy alerts get ignored, so calibrate thresholds to reality and re-baseline after legitimate business changes; a check that stays red hides the next real problem. Route alerts by ownership and severity, to team rotations rather than individuals, with deduplication. Each alert should name the dataset, the check, the observed value against the threshold, and link to the dataset, its lineage and the runbook. When a check stayed silent during a real problem, audit its window, target dataset or branch, execution and routing. Persistently failing checks are triaged one by one: fix the data, or re-baseline or retire a wrong assumption, with an owner for each.

concepts.heading: Investigating with lineage and keys
concepts.body: On a schema alert, trace the change with Data Lineage to where the type first changed and classify it as breaking or not before touching downstream code. For duplicates, deduplicate idempotently where they originate, enforce uniqueness with an expectation on the curated output and watch the upstream duplicate rate. Quality reporting works per dataset: expectation history, check status and incidents, freshness against its SLA, content metrics and owned open issues. A definition of done for publishing a curated dataset includes its documented contract, key expectations, freshness and size checks, alert routing and a runbook.

examPoints: When a scenario shows a successful build that published an empty or duplicated dataset, prefer content checks (row count, size, distinct counts, keys) over relying on build status.

When a scenario describes a blocking expectation catching bad source data before a deadline, prefer keeping the last good version published and escalating to the source owner over overriding the check.

quiz.q: A dataset's latest transaction is fresh every morning, yet users report that the newest events are three days old. Which check would have caught this?
choices: A build-status check confirming that the schedule succeeded
A schema check alerting on any column added to the dataset
A content-freshness check on the maximum event date, plus a freshness check on the upstream source
A health check on the number of files written per transaction
quiz.explain: Transaction time shows that a build ran, not that new data arrived; checking the newest event date and the upstream source detects reprocessed but stale data.

quiz.q: A team's health checks fire dozens of freshness alerts every weekend for a source that never delivers on weekends, and people now ignore them. What should be done?
choices: Delete the freshness checks, because the source is known to be irregular
Send the alerts to more people so someone always responds
Keep the alerts unchanged and add a note to the runbook
Set the freshness threshold to the source's real delivery calendar and route alerts to the owning team
quiz.explain: Calibrating to the real cadence keeps genuine lateness visible while removing noise; deleting or broadcasting alerts makes real problems easier to miss.

days.recap: Keep bad data out with blocking expectations and quarantine, and watch published data with calibrated content, freshness and schema checks whose alerts reach owners with the context to act.

days.title: Organizations, Markings, Roles and Project Structure

concepts.heading: Layered access: organizations, markings and roles
concepts.body: Access in Foundry is layered, and a user must pass every layer: the organization boundary, every marking on the data, and a project role that grants the needed permission. Organizations partition the platform, so cross-organization visibility is restricted by default; a user granted a role on a project in another organization may still not see it. Markings are mandatory access controls: they are conjunctive (a reader needs all of them) and propagate through transform and analysis logic into derived datasets. Project roles such as Viewer, Editor and Owner are discretionary permissions within a project. Neither replaces the other: even the Owner role does not satisfy a marking the user lacks.

concepts.heading: Markings follow the data
concepts.body: Use a marking when a restriction must follow data wherever it is copied or derived, since roles only govern access inside one project. Mark the raw dataset and every derived dataset that still holds sensitive columns. To serve an audience that must not see personal data, publish a separate derived dataset without those columns rather than widening marking membership. An aggregate derived from marked data is published unmarked only after a documented review that it cannot reveal individuals. A single sensitive column can be split into its own keyed, separately protected dataset so the rest of the data stays broadly usable.

concepts.heading: Projects by domain and layer
concepts.body: Separate projects by layer, for example source syncs, transformation pipelines, curated outputs and applications, so each layer has its own audience and role grants expose only what is intended. Independent teams get their own projects and share data through references to published curated outputs, which act as stable interfaces whose producers coordinate changes using lineage. Shared reference data lives in a dedicated shared project readable by the units that consume it. External builders such as consultants can work in an isolated development project with de-identified data, while employees promote changes to production.

concepts.heading: Least privilege through groups
concepts.body: Grant access through groups that hold project roles, not to individuals or shared accounts, so joining or leaving a team updates access cleanly. Replace broad grants such as everyone holding Owner with least-privilege roles, a small owner group and regular access reviews. External parties receive narrow, time-bound access through a dedicated group on a project that holds only the needed data. Broad read access is acceptable only for data classified as non-sensitive, and markings and restricted views stay in force. Never move or unmark sensitive data to make work easier; request the marking through its approval process or use a reviewed de-identified sample.

examPoints: When a scenario has a user with a sufficient project role who still cannot read a dataset, prefer looking for a missing marking or an organization boundary (with Check Access) over granting a higher role.
When a scenario needs one audience to see sensitive columns and another not, prefer a marked full dataset plus an unmarked derived dataset without those columns over widening marking membership.

quiz.q: A colleague holds the Viewer role on a project but cannot open a dataset carrying a marking they do not hold. Which change actually grants access?
choices: Obtaining the marking through its approval process, since markings are required in addition to any role
Promoting the colleague to Owner, the highest project role
Copying the dataset into a project where the colleague is Editor
Removing the marking from the dataset so everyone can read it
quiz.explain: Markings are mandatory and checked in addition to roles; no role substitutes for them, and copying or unmarking data to bypass the control is never acceptable.

quiz.q: A finance analyst transfers to the marketing team and must now be able to read the curated datasets that marketing publishes. Which grant is the cleanest?
choices: Give the analyst Owner on every marketing project
Add the analyst to the marketing consumers group that already holds Viewer on the curated project
Share a team account that already has the right access
Export the curated datasets to a folder the analyst can reach
quiz.explain: Group-based role grants give exactly the intended access and are easy to review and revoke; individual broad roles, shared accounts and exports bypass least privilege.

days.recap: Access requires passing the organization boundary, every marking and a project role; markings follow data into derivatives, and projects split by domain and layer with group-based least privilege.

days.title: Restricted Views, Object Policies and Diagnosing Access

concepts.heading: Restricted views for row-level access
concepts.body: A restricted view is built on a backing dataset and filters rows per reader according to a policy, for example matching a row's region to the user's attribute or granting all rows to members of an "all regions" group. Policies can combine conditions, such as "the row's rep is the user, or the row's team is one the user manages, or the user is in sales operations". Drive policies from attributes synced from the system of record, such as an HR user-to-region mapping, so organizational changes flow through. Enforcing row access at the data layer covers every tool, whereas a filter inside one application module protects only that module. Test a policy with users from every audience after each change, since one AND instead of OR can hide everything.

concepts.heading: What restricted views cannot do
concepts.body: Restricted views cannot be used as an input for transforms, because their rows depend on the reader while pipelines must be reproducible. Pipelines therefore read the backing dataset with a properly granted build identity, and per-audience filtering is applied at the end for readers. Restricted views filter rows only and offer no column-level policies, and their granular policies are discretionary and do not propagate the way markings do. Aggregates computed over a restricted view reflect each viewer's permitted rows, so two users can legitimately see different totals; organization-wide totals are computed from the backing dataset and published after a disclosure review.

concepts.heading: Object and property security in the Ontology
concepts.body: Object and property security policies give row-, column- and cell-level control on object types and are recommended over restricted views for most Ontology use cases. A property that is empty for one user but visible to others points to property-level security or a separately permissioned datasource backing that property, not to the pipeline. An empty link for one user usually means they lack access to the linked object type's backing data. When a healthy pipeline's objects are unreadable for some users, diagnose consumer-side permissions on the backing data and the object type, checked as those users.

concepts.heading: Diagnosing access precisely
concepts.body: The exam guide asks you to explain separately why a user can open a resource, why they can read its data, and why a pipeline can or cannot execute. Check Access shows the specific unmet requirement, such as a marking, role or organization boundary, so you request only that access through the proper path. After a grant, verify with Check Access that the exact identity, for example the build's identity, now satisfies every requirement. Moving a dataset to another project changes which project's roles apply, so re-check consumer and build access afterwards. Stale entitlements found in a review are removed through governed processes, and the offboarding gap that caused them is fixed.

concepts.heading: Proving and reviewing protection
concepts.body: Audits are answered with access configuration history (markings, roles, group membership), Check Access results, lineage showing controls on derived datasets and access logs showing actual reads. An unmarked dataset derived from marked data is a finding to investigate: if sensitive content propagated, apply the marking and assess exposure; if it was de-identified, document the review. Review protection along every lineage path, including derived objects, view policies, export policies and identity scopes, not only at the source. Build identities with excess privilege widen the blast radius, so trim their grants to their actual inputs and outputs.

examPoints: When a scenario needs a pipeline to compute organization-wide results from data that readers see through a restricted view, prefer reading the backing dataset with a granted build identity, since restricted views cannot feed transforms.

When a scenario needs per-user visibility on Ontology objects, including columns or cells, prefer object and property security policies, and use Check Access to diagnose why a specific user sees less.

quiz.q: Regional managers see only their region's rows through a restricted view, and a new transform must compute company-wide totals. What should the transform read?
choices: The restricted view, run by a manager with the widest region
A copy of each manager's view, unioned together nightly
The backing dataset, through a build identity granted access, with results published after review
The Workshop module that already displays the regional totals
quiz.explain: Restricted views cannot be transform inputs because their rows depend on the reader; the pipeline reads the backing dataset under a properly granted identity.

quiz.q: One user sees an object with an empty salary property while colleagues see values for the same object. Where should the investigation start?
choices: The pipeline that builds the backing dataset, which must have dropped the values
The schedule of the object type's backing dataset
The Spark details of the last build
Property security policies, or a separately permissioned datasource for that property, checked with Check Access
quiz.explain: Data that exists for some users but not others is an access question, so property-level security is the first suspect rather than the pipeline.

days.recap: Use restricted views or object security policies to filter what readers see, never as pipeline inputs, and diagnose every access failure with Check Access before granting anything.

days.title: Object Types, Links, Keys and Cardinality

concepts.heading: Entities as object types, relationships as links
concepts.body: Model each real-world entity once as an object type (Order, Customer, Product) and connect them with link types instead of copying one entity's attributes onto another. A many-to-many relationship that carries its own attributes, such as order lines with quantities or a supplier's share in a contract, becomes its own object type keyed by the pair and linked many-to-one to both sides. Events that relate several entities, such as an appointment between a patient and a doctor, are modeled the same way. An object type that tries to hold customer, product and warehouse details on every order is overly broad and duplicates entities.

concepts.heading: Interfaces, shared properties and value types
concepts.body: An interface defines a set of properties that several object types implement, so applications can query all trucks, forklifts and cranes as "assets" without merging or duplicating the types. Shared properties declare a common attribute once, for example a status mapped to a controlled vocabulary in each type's pipeline. Value types define allowed values and formatting once and are reused, which keeps cross-cutting attributes such as money (currency code plus normalized amount) consistent. Fixed-choice attributes become enumerated, validated properties, backed by an expectation in the pipeline.

concepts.heading: Time-varying relationships and attributes
concepts.body: Relationships that change over time, such as which driver is assigned to which vehicle, are modeled as dated assignment objects with start and end dates linked to both sides, plus a derived current link for convenience. Attributes with history, such as prices, become versioned linked objects with an effective range, with the current value derived onto the main entity. This keeps history queryable while applications read current state simply. The derived current values are computed in the pipeline, not maintained by hand.

concepts.heading: Primary keys: unique and stable
concepts.body: Primary keys must come from the entity's identity and survive rebuilds: an employee number assigned once and never changed, a shipment number, or a deterministic hash of only the identifying columns. Positional, random, time-based or mutable values (row numbers, names, email addresses) re-key objects when they change, which detaches user edits and links. Never fill missing keys with placeholders; fix identity upstream or derive a deterministic key, and guard with non-null and uniqueness expectations. Composite keys must be built unambiguously, with escaping or hashing. When several sources feed one object type, namespace the key by source system, or resolve entities through a crosswalk to a canonical id while keeping source ids as properties.

concepts.heading: Link cardinality
concepts.body: Link cardinality must match the real relationship. "Many of these belong to one of those" is a many-to-one link backed by a foreign key, such as each invoice carrying a customer id (equivalently one-to-many from customer to invoice). A one-to-one link cannot represent a carrier that handles many shipments; choosing it is a modeling error. Validate links against the data, for example by checking that foreign keys resolve, and monitor key churn between builds for multi-source object types.

examPoints: When a scenario offers candidate primary keys, prefer an identifier assigned once by the system of record (or a deterministic hash of identifying columns) over names, emails, row numbers or timestamps.
When a scenario describes a relationship that carries its own attributes or changes over time, prefer a separate object type linked to both sides over adding columns to either entity.

quiz.q: Students enrol in many courses, and each enrolment has a grade and a term. How should this be modeled?
choices: An Enrollment object type keyed by student and course, holding grade and term, linked many-to-one to Student and Course
A list of course names stored as a single property on Student
A grade property on Course that is overwritten by each student
One combined object type with every student and course column
quiz.explain: A many-to-many relationship with its own attributes becomes its own object type keyed by the pair and linked to both entities.

quiz.q: A team keys its Customer object type on email address. What is the main risk?
choices: Email addresses are too long to be used in links
Emails can change, which re-keys the object and detaches its history, edits and links
Email addresses cannot be indexed by the Ontology
Emails make the object type visible to other organizations
quiz.explain: A primary key must be immutable; when a mutable attribute changes, the platform sees a new object, so the system of record's stable id should be used and existing objects migrated.

days.recap: Model each entity once with stable, unique keys, express relationships as links with the right cardinality, and give attribute-bearing or time-varying relationships their own linked object types.

days.title: Modeling Anti-patterns, Evolving the Ontology, North or South

concepts.heading: The Ontology models entities, not dashboards
concepts.body: A common anti-pattern is building object types around a dashboard's layout or a pair of entities, then putting entity attributes such as a customer address on them. Attributes belong on the entity's own object type, and dashboards aggregate over links or over a derived aggregate dataset. Aggregates can be materialized as a derived object type keyed by its grain, such as region by month, documented as computed from the source entities and kept alongside them. Rankings and top lists are computed at query time from entity metrics rather than stored as object types. Teams extend one shared Customer type with their own properties or linked satellite types instead of creating duplicates.

concepts.heading: Denormalize minimally and on purpose
concepts.body: Some denormalization helps applications, for example a derived country property on Order so users can filter orders by customer country. Add only the attributes applications filter on, compute them in the pipeline, document them as derived and keep the link to the source entity. This preserves one source of truth while giving fast filtering. Unplanned copies of attributes across types drift out of sync and should be avoided.

concepts.heading: Evolving live resources with Global Branching
concepts.body: The exam guide names Global Branching as the way to change live Ontology resources safely. Develop new properties, renamed links, new object types and their backing datasets on one branch, validate them with the applications pointed at the branch, then merge everything together. Property type changes and renames are breaking for consumers, so find consumers first and change them on the same branch. Adding a property means producing the column with values for all rows and adding it to the object type together. Before raising refresh cadence, verify that builds and indexing keep up, keys stay stable and user edits are preserved.

concepts.heading: Keys, edits and backing data during change
concepts.body: Changing a primary key, splitting an object type or retiring one is a migration of identity: map old keys to new, migrate edits and links, update consumers, validate on a branch, then deprecate with a short overlap. Even a small change to key derivation, such as trimming whitespace, can re-key objects and detach edits, so treat key logic as part of the identity contract and monitor key churn. After a logic change, diff the key sets between builds and restore objects removed by mistake. A backing dataset must have exactly one current row per key; incremental outputs that append corrections need a keyed merge and a uniqueness expectation.

concepts.heading: North or south of the Ontology
concepts.body: South of the Ontology means computing in the pipeline and materializing the result as a property; north means computing at interaction time in applications or functions. Values that are deterministic, widely used, needed for filtering or sorting, and fine with periodic freshness belong south, with a formula version recorded so every consumer sees the same number. Hypothetical or user-input-dependent values, such as a what-if delivery date while a user edits an order in Workshop, belong north. Mixed cases split naturally: materialize a filterable score south and generate an on-demand explanation north. The placement criteria are consistency, reuse and freshness.

examPoints: When a scenario changes a live object type that applications depend on, prefer developing the change and its consumers on a Global Branching branch and merging together over editing production directly.

When a scenario asks where a widely used, deterministic value should be computed, prefer south of the Ontology (pipeline, materialized property); when it depends on user input at interaction time, prefer north.

quiz.q: A risk score is needed by three applications for filtering and sorting, must be identical everywhere and can refresh nightly. Where should it be computed?
choices: In each application's display logic when a user opens a page
In a separate spreadsheet that analysts upload weekly
South of the Ontology, in the pipeline, materialized as a property with its formula version recorded
North of the Ontology, recomputed by an AI model on every query
quiz.explain: Consistent, reusable, filterable values with periodic freshness are computed once in the pipeline and exposed as properties.

quiz.q: After a pipeline change trimmed whitespace from a key column, users report that their edits disappeared from some objects. What happened?
choices: The object type's indexing failed and needs a manual retry
Users lost their permissions on the object type
The applications cached an old version of the objects
The trimmed keys re-identified those objects, detaching edits, so old keys must be mapped to new ones and edits re-attached
quiz.explain: Key derivation is part of object identity; changing it creates new objects, so a mapping migration and key-churn monitoring are required.

days.recap: Model entities rather than dashboards, evolve live Ontology resources on Global Branching with key-safe migrations, and compute shared deterministic values south and interactive ones north.

days.title: AI Assistants and Pipeline-layer AI Enrichment

concepts.heading: Different AI aids for different jobs
concepts.body: The exam guide asks you to distinguish AI FDE, AIP Assist, Continue and data-producing LLM or embedding transforms. Code assistants (Continue in code environments, AI FDE as an engineering assistant) help engineers write, change and debug pipelines; their output is code and configuration that goes through normal review and tests. AIP Assist answers questions about using the platform. LLM and embedding transforms run models over data inside a pipeline to produce columns such as classifications, summaries or vectors at build time. Matching the tool to the job is a frequent exam theme.

concepts.heading: Assistants propose, engineers decide
concepts.body: Code assistants are useful for drafting transforms, explaining errors and orienting in an unfamiliar pipeline, but the engineer stays accountable. Any fix an assistant suggests is applied on a branch with tests, branch validation and review before release, never as an automatic production edit. A summary of an unfamiliar pipeline produced by an assistant is verified against lineage and the code before changes. AI FDE acts in the user's own session and needs user consent for writes. The value of assistants is measured by delivery and quality outcomes (lead time, defects caught, incidents), not by usage.

concepts.heading: Deterministic logic first, AI for bounded interpretation
concepts.body: Use deterministic logic for explicit rules and AI for bounded interpretation of unstructured data, combining them where useful. Address parsing, for example, uses reference data and rules as the primary method, with an LLM only for the residual records the rules cannot handle, validated and audited. Text-to-category tasks, free-text normalization and embeddings for search are good fits for pipeline AI. Rules that can be stated precisely stay deterministic because they are cheaper, testable and exact.

concepts.heading: Structured output and deterministic post-processing
concepts.body: AI-produced columns need a constrained schema: an enumerated category, a range-constrained integer, a number plus a currency field, or an ISO-8601 date. Code then normalizes and validates the result, and anything unparseable or ambiguous (such as 3/4/2026) is flagged for review instead of guessed. Parse failures are kept with a failure status and the raw response, excluded from consumer-facing properties and counted. Invalid values are never silently defaulted. AI-extracted join keys are typed, normalized and validated against the reference dataset they join to.

concepts.heading: Caching, provenance and governance
concepts.body: Cache AI results keyed by input content and prompt version so unchanged rows are not paid for twice, and backfill older rows gradually when the prompt changes. Record the prompt version, model and raw response per row, plus a reason field when classifications must be explainable. Treat each model call as a governed data flow: confirm the model is enabled for that data class, minimize and redact what is sent, and keep prompts and responses under the source's markings. When AI-derived values drive access control, validate strictly, default to the safe side and document the decision. Monitor AI steps with validation-failure rates, output distributions, sampled human review and a fixed evaluation set re-run on changes.

examPoints: When a scenario needs a new column for every row (a category, a summary, an embedding), prefer an LLM or embedding transform in the pipeline; when it needs help writing or debugging the pipeline, prefer a code assistant; for platform how-to questions, prefer AIP Assist.

When a scenario adds an AI step to a pipeline, prefer constrained structured output, deterministic validation, caching by input and prompt version, and recorded provenance over trusting free-text model output.

quiz.q: An engineer wants help understanding a stack trace from a failing transform in a code repository. Which aid fits best?
choices: A code assistant such as Continue or AI FDE that reads the error and code and proposes a diagnosis for the engineer to review
An LLM transform that adds an explanation column to the failing dataset
An embedding transform that indexes the repository's files
A health check that alerts when the stack trace appears again
quiz.explain: Interactive debugging is a code assistant's job; transforms produce data columns, and the engineer still reviews and owns the fix.

quiz.q: An LLM step extracts invoice dates as free text, and downstream joins fail on mixed formats. What is the best remedy?
choices: Ask every consumer to parse the dates in their own way
Request ISO-8601 dates in the output schema, parse deterministically, validate ranges and flag ambiguous values for review
Switch to a larger model and keep the free-text output
Replace unparseable dates with the processing date
quiz.explain: Constrained output plus deterministic parsing and validation produces reliable typed data; pushing parsing to consumers or defaulting values silently corrupts results.

days.recap: Use code assistants to build, AIP Assist to learn the platform and LLM transforms to produce data, and wrap every AI step in structured output, validation, caching, provenance and governance.

days.title: Choosing the AI Layer and Reviewing AI-Generated Work

concepts.heading: Pipeline-layer versus Ontology-layer AI
concepts.body: The exam guide asks you to choose pipeline-layer AI for reusable batch enrichment and Ontology-layer AI for interactive, context-dependent reasoning. Tagging every contract with a risk category, normalizing supplier names or classifying tickets for routing are reusable, row-wise results that belong in the pipeline and become properties. A free-form question a user asks about one document or customer while viewing it is answered on demand at the application layer, for example with AIP Logic. The two combine well: the pipeline provides a baseline summary for every record, and an Action regenerates one record on demand.

concepts.heading: Embeddings and semantic search
concepts.body: Index-building AI work belongs in the pipeline: an embedding transform writes a vector column that is exposed as a vector property on the object type. At search time the application embeds the user's query and searches that property. The data engineer owns the embedding pipeline and the vector property; the application side owns the query experience. Keeping embeddings in the pipeline means they are computed once, refreshed with the data and governed like any other column.

concepts.heading: Role boundary for AI work
concepts.body: The exam guide's role boundary places pipelines, curated data, Ontology data modeling and pipeline-layer AI with the data engineer, and agents, prompts and interactive AI with the AI engineer. When an agent depends on order data, the data engineer guarantees the curated objects, links, freshness and quality, plus any batch enrichment, while agent instructions, tools and conversation evaluation belong to AI engineering. A shared contract states which properties the agent may rely on. Distractors often push the data engineer into owning the agent itself.
